idiom_name: hand-written pair of conversion functions over a flat message struct (no reflection)
implementation_notes: ISO C has no reflection, no serialisation layer and no runtime type names, so the messaging mapper is a pair of functions per pair - order_to_msg(const struct order *, struct order_msg *) and order_from_msg(const struct order_msg *, struct order *) - living in one translation unit whose header is the only file that includes both the domain header and the wire header. The functions flatten the aggregate deliberately (references become ids, money becomes minor units) while the wire encoding of the flat message struct is a separate step (cJSON, msgpack-c, or a fixed-width record). What replaces the classic mapper class is that translation unit; keep ownership documented, because whoever allocates the message's strings must also free them.
pitfalls: Strings and buffers the mapper allocates need one documented owner: a strdup() per message leaks unless the message destructor frees it.
Nothing ties the struct fields to the wire keys, so adding a field on either side silently leaves the mapper stale - pin golden payloads in tests.
A message struct that reuses domain pointers invites receivers to reach into the domain through the message; copy or borrow with an explicit contract.
Numeric fields need explicit width and byte-order handling (htons/htonl) whenever the channel format differs from the host's.
